base_text: Different people describe how they each became homeless.

variants.text: When the factory I had worked at for eleven years closed, I could not find anything else for months. My savings went on rent until there was nothing left, and by spring I was three months behind and out on the pavement. I slept in stairwells and bus shelters, and my chest got so bad I could barely stand. A drop-in centre finally gave me a mat and a meal, but every job I applied for wanted an address I did not have.

variants.perspective: someone who fell ill and lost their income
variants.text: It started when I got ill and could not work; the sick pay ran out, then the bills piled up. I chose food and medicine over rent, and once I missed two payments the eviction came quickly. I lived in my car until it was towed, then in a tent behind the retail park. Being outside made my condition far worse, and without a permanent address the agency kept bouncing my benefit claim.

variants.perspective: a woman who fled domestic violence with her children
variants.text: I left with my kids and a bag of clothes because staying was not safe any more. With no money of my own and nowhere to go, we ended up in a friend's spare room, then a hostel, then a night in the car. The stress and the constant moving wrecked my health and the children's schooling. Everyone kept telling me to get a tenancy, but you cannot get one with no deposit and no fixed address.

variants.perspective: a working person priced out by a rent hike
variants.text: I never stopped working, but when the landlord sold up the new rent was almost double and I simply could not cover it. Nothing else in the city was affordable on my wage, so when the notice ran out I had nowhere to move to. I started sleeping in the back of the shop and washing at the gym. People assume you must have done something wrong, but I had a job the whole time; I just could not find a room I could pay for.

After my relapse I lost the job, and not long after that I lost the people who had been putting up with me. Once the drinking took over I stopped opening the letters, and the arrears turned into an eviction before I really understood what was happening. I was on the streets for the best part of a year, and out there it only got harder to stay clean. The shelter took me in and pointed me to treatment, but getting work with a gap that big and no address felt impossible.

My depression got to the point where I could not keep up with anything: not the job, not the forms, not the rent. When my benefits were stopped over some paperwork I did not manage to send, the money vanished and the eviction notice came. I ended up sleeping rough, and being out there pulled me down further than I had ever been. A support worker got me a hostel place, but every application still trips on the same thing: no fixed address.
